---
title: "Quiz: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. RL step: $x \leftarrow x \cdot A^\top\big(y/(Ax + b)\big)$, with $A$ = blur by a PSF that sums to 1 and $b$ = background.

---

**Q1.** Why can a Richardson–Lucy estimate never become negative, if it starts positive and the data are non-negative?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What kind of operations does one step consist of?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
One step multiplies each pixel by a sum of non-negative numbers (ratios of non-negative data to positive model values, weighted by the non-negative PSF). A product of non-negative factors stays non-negative. Linear filters subtract, and can go below zero.
:::

---

**Q2.** RL starts from a flat image with the mean of the data. After one step, what is the total of the estimate (no background)?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Flux is kept every step.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The same as the total of the data: RL keeps the total number of photons at every iteration (for a PSF that sums to 1). The flat start already has this total, and each step keeps it.
:::

---

**Q3.** You run RL on a noisy image and watch the error against a known truth. It falls for 20 iterations, then rises. What is happening, and what do you do with real data where the truth is unknown?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which frequencies come in late?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Semi-convergence: early iterations restore the strong low frequencies, later ones the weak high frequencies, which are mostly noise, so the estimate starts fitting the noise (speckles). With real data: stop when the blurred estimate fits the data to the noise level (misfit about 1 per pixel), or choose the number of iterations on a test sample (beads, phantom) with the same noise, or add a penalty.
:::

---

**Q4.** The same specimen is imaged once with 1000 and once with 100 photons per pixel. For which image should you stop RL earlier?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where does the noise start to dominate?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
For the 100-photon image: its relative noise is larger, so the frequencies that carry mostly noise start at a lower frequency, and RL reaches them after fewer iterations. In the demo's bead image: best at 8 iterations with 100 photons, at 40 with 1000.
:::

---

**Q5.** After RL the dark background of an image has become full of bright dots, and the camera offset had not been subtracted. Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does RL do with light it cannot attribute to a background?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Without a background term, the constant offset must be explained as object light. RL's estimates are built of sharp bright points (it maximises a Poisson likelihood with no smoothness), so the uniform level is concentrated into dots. Subtract the offset, and put the remaining background in the model ($Ax + b$).
:::

---

**Q6.** In a deconvolved widefield stack, a thin membrane parallel to the coverslip is still smeared over a micrometre in z, while a filament running along z is sharp. Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where are the frequencies of a horizontal sheet, and what does the widefield OTF miss?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A horizontal sheet is uniform in $x$ and $y$, so all its frequencies lie on the $k_z$ axis ($k_x = k_y = 0$). The widefield OTF is zero in a cone around that axis (the missing cone): those frequencies were never recorded, so no deconvolution can restore them. The vertical filament's frequencies lie mostly in the $k_x$, $k_y$ directions, which the OTF covers.
:::

---

**Q7.** A deconvolution makes small beads look sharper and smaller than in any other image, with a dark ring around each. What do you suspect?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which way was the PSF wrong?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The PSF used is too wide: the method removes more blur than there was, over-sharpening the beads (too small) and digging dark halos around them. A PSF that is too narrow does the opposite: it leaves blur and looks "safe".
:::

---

**Q8.** Why does blind deconvolution without constraints tend to return the blurred image itself?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Is there a PSF and an object that explain the data perfectly without any deblurring?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
"PSF = a single point, object = the observed image" reproduces the data exactly, so the likelihood has no reason to prefer the true pair. Alternating updates drift towards this trivial solution. Constraints (limited size, smoothness, a parametric shape, a known width) are needed to rule it out, and even then a good starting PSF matters.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Show that one RL step without background keeps the total, $\sum_j x_j^{\text{new}} = \sum_i y_i$, using $A^\top\mathbf 1 = \mathbf 1$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Write $\sum_j x_j [A^\top r]_j = \sum_i r_i (A\mathbf x)_i$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
With $r_i = y_i/(A\mathbf x)_i$: $\sum_j x_j^{\text{new}} = \sum_j x_j \sum_i A_{ij} r_i = \sum_i r_i \sum_j A_{ij}x_j = \sum_i \frac{y_i}{(A\mathbf x)_i}(A\mathbf x)_i = \sum_i y_i$. ($A^\top\mathbf 1 = \mathbf 1$ is what makes the flat start's total equal to the data total, and gives the update its fixed-point form.)
:::
